The data come from clinical sources and are intended for research use.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.
Data contamination is a potential concern for all benchmarks of this kind.

Ground truth is isolated from runtime agent access: labels reside in an independent evaluation service disconnected from the agent sandbox with no network route, and the repository does not publish them.

The environment is frozen at release: the database snapshot, the software image and the simulated-patient language model are all pinned to fixed versions, and no external service is called at evaluation time other than the model under test.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
The grader checks both the intended state changes and that all other records remain unchanged, so out-of-scope modifications are detected and counted as failures.
We validated the automatic evaluator on 200 outputs labelled by two physicians; agreement was 94%, with a false-positive rate of 3% and a false-negative rate of 8%.
Every run applies temperature 0 with a fixed seed. The main text describes the policy of executing each task three times.

We report 95% confidence intervals computed by bootstrapping over tasks, so the resampling unit is the task; where several tasks share a patient, we resample patients instead to account for clustering.
Our results were obtained from a single run of each model.
API calls used snapshot IDs gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 with temperature 0 and 2,048-token output ceiling. All reported results match harness version v1.2.0.
The agent can use tools to interact with the environment.

We ran conformance tests confirming that each tool behaves as documented. Two tools are simulated stubs that return fixed placeholder responses; this is disclosed in the paper and also stated in the tool descriptions shown to the agent.
Accuracy is reported by task family (diagnosis, ordering, documentation) and by patient subgroup (sex, race), with case counts displayed for every slice in the tables.

The patient records utilized are genuine, de-identified entries sourced from a hospital database. Their usage was authorized via a data use agreement that mandated credentialed access and de-identification compliant with the safe harbour method. Additionally, the data are distributed under terms distinct from the MIT code licence.
